issues.body:
### Describe the bug

If `tauri.conf.json` is saved with a UTF-8 byte order mark (`EF BB BF`), Tauri fails to
parse it and reports a generic JSON syntax error pointing at line 1, column 1. The file is
valid JSON and looks completely correct in an editor, so the actual cause (an invisible
leading byte) is not discoverable from the error message.

This is easy to hit on Windows, because PowerShell — the default shell — writes a BOM for
several common encoding options. Any script or tooling that regenerates or rewrites the
config can silently introduce it.

### Reproduction

1. Create a Tauri v2 app.
2. Rewrite the config with PowerShell, which prepends a BOM:
   ```powershell
   $c = Get-Content tauri.conf.json -Raw
   Set-Content tauri.conf.json -Value $c -Encoding UTF8
   ```
3. Verify the BOM is present:
   ```
   $ xxd tauri.conf.json | head -1
   00000000: efbb bf7b 0a20 2022 2473 6368 656d 6122  ...{.  "$schema"
   ```
4. Run any command that loads the config (e.g. `cargo tauri build`).

### Expected behavior

The config is parsed normally. A UTF-8 BOM is a legal way to encode a UTF-8 file, and most
JSON consumers either skip it or say explicitly that it is the problem.

### Actual behavior

Parsing fails with a `serde_json` syntax error at line 1 column 1. Nothing in the message
mentions a BOM or an encoding issue, and the file renders as valid JSON in every editor,
so the failure looks like config corruption rather than an encoding problem.

### Root cause

In `tauri-utils` (2.9.3), `src/config/parse.rs`:

- `:282` — `let raw = read_to_string(&path)?;` — this wraps `std::fs::read_to_string`
  (`:393`), which validates UTF-8 but does **not** strip a BOM: `U+FEFF` is valid UTF-8 and
  is kept in the returned `String`.
- `:351-355` — `do_parse_json` passes `raw` straight to `serde_json::from_str` with no
  normalization:
  ```rust
  fn do_parse_json<D: DeserializeOwned>(raw: &str, path: &Path) -> Result<D, ConfigError> {
    serde_json::from_str(raw).map_err(|error| ConfigError::FormatJson {
      path: path.into(),
      error,
    })
  }
  ```
- `serde_json` rejects the leading `U+FEFF` and reports `expected value at line 1 column 1`.

Note that when the `config-json5` feature is enabled, `:288-300` tries JSON5 first and, on
failure, falls back to reporting the `serde_json` error — so the surfaced message is the
same either way. The comment there already anticipates that this can be confusing.

### Suggested fix

Strip a leading BOM once, right after the file is read, so every format path benefits:

```rust
let raw = read_to_string(&path)?;
let raw = raw.strip_prefix('\u{feff}').unwrap_or(&raw).to_string();
```

Alternatively, do it inside the `read_to_string` helper at `:393`, which also covers the
`.json5` (`:306`) and `.toml` (`:318`) branches.

If stripping is not desirable, detecting the BOM and returning a dedicated error that names
it would at least make the failure diagnosable.

### Platform and versions

- OS: Windows 11 (also reproducible anywhere a BOM-prefixed config is produced)
- Tauri: v2 (`tauri = "2"`, `tauri-build = "2"`)
- `tauri-utils`: 2.9.3
- Config schema: `https://schema.tauri.app/config/2`

### Prior art

`serde_json` deliberately does not skip BOMs, so consumers are expected to handle it. Other
tools in this space normalize it at the read boundary for exactly this reason. #15601 notes
a related BOM pitfall elsewhere in the Tauri toolchain (`latest.json` must be written
BOM-free), which suggests handling this once at the config read boundary would remove a
recurring class of confusing failures.

I'm happy to open a PR with the fix above if you'd like.
issues.title: [bug] `tauri.conf.json` fails to parse if the file starts with a UTF-8 BOM

issues.body:
## Describe the problem

A plugin author cannot get a value set on their own Rust `Builder` into their Android or iOS plugin. The only configuration a native plugin receives comes from the app's `tauri.conf.json`.

`Plugin::initialize` builds the `PluginApi` from the config Tauri read out of `plugins.<name>`, and `register_android_plugin` / `register_ios_plugin` forward that same `raw_config` to the native `load()`:

```rust
// tauri/src/plugin.rs:799
raw_config: Arc::new(config.clone()),

// tauri/src/plugin/mobile.rs:172 and :262
let config = self.raw_config.clone();
```

`raw_config` is private, only ever assigned in `initialize`, and `plugin::Builder` exposes no method to contribute to it. The path is closed by construction.

This matters because a Rust builder is the idiomatic way to configure a Tauri plugin — `tauri-plugin-log`, `tauri-plugin-updater`, `tauri-plugin-store` and `tauri-plugin-window-state` all use one — but the pattern stops working the moment a plugin has a native mobile implementation. And `tauri.conf.json` can only hold a literal, so a value like `concat!("my-app/", env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION"))`, or one read from an environment variable or a Cargo feature, cannot be expressed there at all.

It looks like nobody has solved this so much as avoided it: across `plugins-workspace`, `opener` is the only plugin with both a plugin-owned Rust `Builder` and a native mobile layer, and its builder field never crosses the bridge.

## Describe the solution you'd like

Additive methods on `PluginApi` that take the config at the registration call site:

```rust
let handle = api.register_android_plugin_with_config(
   "org.example.plugin", "ExamplePlugin",
   serde_json::json!({ "userAgent": user_agent }),
)?;
```

- **No native-side change.** Android's `Plugin.getConfig(Class)` and Swift's `parseConfig(_:)` already consume this exact JSON string.
- **No merge policy to invent.** A `Builder::default_config()` merged with `tauri.conf.json` raises questions with no obviously right answer — which side wins, and is the merge deep or shallow. At the registration site the author already has `api.config()` in scope and can merge however the plugin wants.
- **Purely additive.** Existing `register_*_plugin` behaviour is unchanged.

A `Builder::mobile_config(impl Serialize)` populating `raw_config` before registration would work too, and reads better at the definition site. Either is fine; merge semantics are the only reason to prefer the explicit one.

## Alternatives considered

**Push the value with a plugin command after registration** — the current workaround. Define a native `configure` command and invoke it from `setup()` right after `register_*_plugin`, via `run_mobile_plugin`.

It works, and the ordering is safe: registration blocks until the native plugin is loaded, and `setup()` runs before the event loop exists, so it lands before the webview can invoke anything. `run_mobile_plugin` also bypasses the ACL, so the command needs no `build.rs` `COMMANDS` entry or permission and stays unreachable from JS. The costs:

- The same boilerplate command in Kotlin **and** Swift for every plugin that needs it.
- A failed push propagates out of `setup()`, aborting plugin initialisation — and with the `.expect(...)` every documented bootstrap uses, panicking the app at launch. That is harsh for what may be a cosmetic setting, with nowhere obvious to degrade gracefully.
- It is undiscoverable. Nothing in the plugin-development docs suggests it and no official plugin demonstrates it, so each author rediscovers the limitation from the Tauri source and reinvents the same fix.

**Require `tauri.conf.json`** — what the ecosystem does today. Rules out computed values, and splits a plugin's configuration across two places when it also has Rust-side options.

**Keep the implementation in Rust and skip the native plugin** — how `tauri-plugin-http` sidesteps the problem entirely, with no `android/` or `ios/` directory. Not available to plugins that exist precisely because they need platform APIs.

issues.body:
### Describe the problem

When running Tauri mobile development commands and multiple physical devices or simulators are available, Tauri may automatically select one device instead of interactively asking the developer which device should be used.

This can be inconvenient when both a physical device and a simulator are available.

## Example: iOS

My development machine had both a physical iPhone and an iOS Simulator available:

```text
== Devices ==

MacBook Pro de Luis
iPhone de Luis (17.7.1)

== Simulators ==

iPhone 15 (26.3.1)
```

The iPhone simulator had the identifier:

```text
76BDA1C1-2D8E-415A-A57B-939EE4C71599
```

The physical iPhone was also available to Xcode, including wireless connectivity.

Running:

```bash
npm run tauri ios dev
```

could select the physical device automatically.

To use the simulator, I had to explicitly provide the device:

```bash
npm run tauri ios dev -- "76BDA1C1-2D8E-415A-A57B-939EE4C71599"
```

## Expected behavior

When multiple compatible destinations are available, Tauri could optionally display an interactive selection:

```text
Multiple devices found:

1. iPhone de Luis (iOS 17.7.1) [physical]
2. iPhone 15 (iOS 26.3.1) [simulator]

Select device:
>
```

The selected destination would then be used for the development session.

## Why this is useful

Physical iOS devices can remain available to Xcode over Wi-Fi even after the USB cable has been disconnected.

For example:

```text
Physical iPhone: connected
iOS Simulator: booted
```

In this situation, automatic selection may not match the developer's intention.

The same situation can occur with multiple Android devices/emulators.

## Desired behavior

When more than one valid device is detected:

1. Detect all available devices.
2. Show their platform, type and name.
3. Allow the developer to select one interactively.
4. Continue normally after selection.

A non-interactive option should still be available for scripts/CI, for example:

```bash
tauri ios dev "<UDID>"
```

which already provides an explicit way to select a destination.

## Cross-platform scope

This would be useful for both:

```text
iOS
- physical devices
- simulators

Android
- physical devices
- emulators
```

## Related discussion

There is already a Tauri discussion proposing simulator/device pre-selection via the command line, including the problem of working with multiple simulators:

https://github.com/tauri-apps/tauri/discussions/9664

## Expected outcome

Tauri should provide a convenient interactive destination-selection experience when multiple mobile devices are available, while preserving explicit device selection for automation and CI.


### Describe the solution you'd like

My development machine had both a physical iPhone and an iOS Simulator available:

Multiple devices found:

1. iPhone de Luis (iOS 17.7.1) [physical]
2. iPhone 15 (iOS 26.3.1) [simulator]

Select device:
>

### Alternatives considered

_No response_

### Additional context

_No response_

issues.body:
## Describe the problem

`tauri::menu` is gated behind `#[cfg(desktop)]` (`crates/tauri/src/lib.rs`, checked in 2.11.5), so there is no menu API on iOS.

That gate predates iPadOS 26, which now synthesizes a menu bar for every app. An iPad running a Tauri app therefore *shows* a menu bar — File, Edit, View, Window, Help — that the app has no way to reach. It contains only the system defaults, and there is no supported way to add an item, remove one, or respond to a selection.

The gap is confusing in a specific way: the **same** File menu appears on macOS and on iPadOS, and on macOS I can add to it in about twenty lines. On iPadOS I cannot add to it at all. Users see the menu, reasonably expect the app's commands in it, and the app can't put them there.

This matters beyond cosmetics. In our app every dashboard action — import, export, rename, duplicate, delete — is reached through a right-click context menu. There is no right-click on iPad, so the system menu bar is the natural home for those commands, and it is the one place we cannot put them.

## Describe the solution you'd like

Make `tauri::menu` available on iOS, backed by UIKit's menu building API (`UIResponder.buildMenu(with:)` / `UIMenuBuilder`), so the existing types work on iPadOS as they do on desktop:

```rust
let menu = Menu::default(app)?;
let item = MenuItem::with_id(app, "import", "Import…", true, None::<&str>)?;
// locate the File submenu, then:
submenu.insert(&item, 0)?;
app.set_menu(menu)?;
```

with `on_menu_event` delivering selections exactly as it does today on desktop.

A reduced subset would already solve most of this: **insert items into the system-provided menus, and receive their events.** Fuller parity — custom top-level submenus, dynamic enable/disable, accelerators — could follow later.

## Alternatives considered

- **Native Swift in `gen/apple/`** — override `buildMenu(with:)` in the generated Xcode project and bridge selections back to Rust. This works, but it means hand-maintaining generated output and writing a bespoke bridge in every app that wants a menu item.
- **In-app UI instead** — an HTML toolbar or overflow menu. Perfectly fine, and what we will likely do near-term, but it ignores a menu bar the user can already see, and gives up hardware-keyboard shortcuts.
- **Long-press to raise `contextmenu`** — unreliable in WKWebView; it races the native selection callout, so it is not something to build a primary interaction on.

## Additional context

- Tauri 2.11.5.
- Verified directly: `pub mod menu` carries `#[cfg(desktop)]`.
- macOS confirmed working in our app via `Menu::default` → `Submenu::insert` → `AppHandle::set_menu`.
- The iPadOS menu bar was observed on a physical iPad running our Tauri app.
- Related iPadOS 26 chrome that is likewise not addressable from Tauri today: #11475 (SafeArea control) and #15521 (window controls overlapping content).
issues.title: [feat] Menu support on iOS/iPadOS (UIMenuBuilder), matching the macOS menu API

issues.body:
### Describe the problem

The NSIS uninstaller always shows a **"Delete the application data"** checkbox on the confirm page, and there is no way to hide it or change what it removes.

When ticked, it deletes exactly two hardcoded paths:

```nsis
SetShellVarContext current
RmDir /r "$APPDATA\${BUNDLEID}"
RmDir /r "$LOCALAPPDATA\${BUNDLEID}"
```

That is correct for apps that store data through Tauri's own path APIs under the bundle identifier. It is silently a no-op for apps that don't.

Our case: the app ships a sidecar service that owns the database and OAuth tokens, and it stores them under `%APPDATA%\<ProductName>` rather than `%APPDATA%\<bundle.identifier>`. The uninstaller therefore offers users a checkbox that destroys nothing, on a page most people click straight through. A control that claims to do something and does nothing is worse than no control, so we would rather remove it than leave it misleading.

### Describe the solution you'd like

A field on `NsisConfig`, e.g.:

```json
{ "bundle": { "windows": { "nsis": { "deleteAppDataOnUninstall": false } } } }
```

`false` would omit the checkbox from the confirm page entirely (not merely leave it unticked). Optionally, an extended form taking explicit paths would also solve it for apps that do have app data to remove, just not at the bundle-identifier location.

### Alternatives considered

Neither is good, which is why this is worth a config field.

**1. `bundle.windows.nsis.template` — fork the whole template.** Supported and explicit, but it means vendoring the installer script and re-diffing it on every upgrade. `installer.nsi` has changed meaningfully several times across 2.x (NSIS 3.8 to 3.11, plugin signing, `!addplugindir`, DPI, RTL). Drift is silent: a stale fork keeps building and just stops receiving fixes. That is a large, permanent maintenance burden to remove one checkbox.

**2. `!macroundef MUI_UNPAGE_CONFIRM` from an installer hook, re-declared without the custom SHOW/LEAVE functions.** Five lines, and it works, but it depends on MUI2 internals that are not public API in either NSIS or Tauri, it emits an unused-function warning on every build, and it silently drops `un.SkipIfPassive` from the confirm page unless that is re-added by hand.

Overriding the wiring directly is not possible: the checkbox is created in `un.ConfirmShow` and attached with a plain `!define MUI_PAGE_CUSTOMFUNCTION_SHOW`, and `!define` on an existing symbol is a fatal `PS_ERROR` rather than an override. The four `NSIS_HOOK_*` macros all fire inside `Section` bodies, long after the confirm page has been shown and left, so hooks give no leverage either.

### Additional context

Checked `NsisConfig` on `@tauri-apps/cli` 2.11.4 (current): 14 fields, none related to app data.

`template`, `headerImage`, `sidebarImage`, `installerIcon`, `uninstallerIcon`, `uninstallerHeaderImage`, `installMode`, `languages`, `customLanguageFiles`, `displayLanguageSelector`, `compression`, `startMenuFolder`, `installerHooks`, `minimumWebview2Version`

Relevant template lines on `dev`: checkbox variables and `un.ConfirmShow` around 425 to 463, deletion block around 869 to 883.

Happy to open a PR if the shape above sounds right.
issues.title: [feat] NSIS: allow disabling the "Delete the application data" checkbox

issues.body:
### Describe the problem

If you use the uninstaller in silent mode (parameter `/S`), there is no option to enable the deletion of the application data.

### Describe the solution you'd like

~~Add an option to tauri.conf.json that allows this behaviour to be controlled.~~
I suggest adding an uninstaller CLI flag /DELETEAPPDATA.

**Why a CLI flag instead of a config option:**
- Whether app data should be removed is usually decided by whoever runs the uninstaller (e.g. a package manager like Chocolatey, or an IT deployment script), not at build time.
- It matches how the other uninstaller options (/P, /UPDATE) already work.
- The change is small and self-contained in installer.nsi.

**Proposed behaviour:**
- uninstall.exe /S /DELETEAPPDATA (or /P /DELETEAPPDATA) deletes the app data, just like checking "Delete the application data" in the UI.
- In interactive mode, /DELETEAPPDATA pre-checks that checkbox. The user can still uncheck it.
- It has no effect together with /UPDATE, which keeps the current behaviour of never deleting app data during updates.

### Alternatives considered

The behaviour can already be achieved today with the NSIS installer hooks (bundle > windows > nsis > installerHooks), since NSIS_HOOK_PREUNINSTALL runs before the app data check:

```
!macro NSIS_HOOK_PREUNINSTALL
  ${GetOptions} $CMDLINE "/DELETEAPPDATA" $R0
  ${IfNot} ${Errors}
    StrCpy $DeleteAppDataCheckboxState 1
  ${EndIf}
!macroend
```


Caveat: This relies on the internal Tauri variable $DeleteAppDataCheckboxState and may break with any Tauri update

### Additional context

_No response_

issues.body:
### Describe the problem

This is specific to `svelte` & `sveltekit` and might not benefit anyone else outside of those using this framework.

When sending an `ipc` request as part of a `sveltekit` [`load`](https://svelte.dev/docs/kit/load#Making-fetch-requests) function `svelte` will complain that:

```
Loading ipc://localhost/TauRPC__Provider.get_providers using `window.fetch`. For best results, use the `fetch` that is passed to your `load` function: https://svelte.dev/docs/kit/load#making-fetch-requests
```

This is because the `sendIpcMessage()` uses the native `fetch()` of the webview in use.

```ts
function sendIpcMessage(message) {
    const { cmd, callback, error, payload, options } = message

    if (
      !customProtocolIpcFailed
      && (canUseCustomProtocol || cmd === fetchChannelDataCommand)
    ) {
      const { contentType, data } = processIpcMessage(payload)

      const headers = new Headers((options && options.headers) || {})
      headers.set('Content-Type', contentType)
      headers.set('Tauri-Callback', callback)
      headers.set('Tauri-Error', error)
      headers.set('Tauri-Invoke-Key', __TAURI_INVOKE_KEY__)

      fetch(window.__TAURI_INTERNALS__.convertFileSrc(cmd, 'ipc'), {
        method: 'POST',
        body: data,
        headers
      })
```

`Svelte` however, would like you to use their supplied `fetch` as it offers the following & even warns that things might be inconsistent or otherwise affected when not used:

```
fetch: {
    (input: RequestInfo | URL, init?: RequestInit): Promise<Response>;
    (input: string | URL | Request, init?: RequestInit): Promise<Response>;
}

fetch is equivalent to the [native fetch web API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/fetch), with a few additional features:

    It can be used to make credentialed requests on the server, as it inherits the cookie and authorization headers for the page request.
    It can make relative requests on the server (ordinarily, fetch requires a URL with an origin when used in a server context).
    Internal requests (e.g. for +server.js routes) go directly to the handler function when running on the server, without the overhead of an HTTP call.
    During server-side rendering, the response will be captured and inlined into the rendered HTML by hooking into the text and json methods of the Response object. Note that headers will not be serialized, unless explicitly included via [filterSerializedResponseHeaders](https://svelte.dev/docs/kit/hooks#handle)
    During hydration, the response will be read from the HTML, guaranteeing consistency and preventing an additional network request.

You can learn more about making credentialed requests with cookies [here](https://svelte.dev/docs/kit/load#Cookies)
``` 

### Describe the solution you'd like

I'm not too familiar with the internals of `tauri`, but maybe it is possible to allow `invoke` to accept a custom `fetch` implementation for specific cases like these.

The already exists an `InvokeOptions` interface for `invoke` calls to add custom headers if necessary. This could perhaps be extended to also accept an implementation of `fetch`

### Alternatives considered

The only alternatives to suppress these `warnings` are to 
- not use `sveltekits` [`load`](https://svelte.dev/docs/kit/load) functions for any request made using `tauri's` `ipc` mechanism & integrate them as regular calls within the components which required them
or
- simply ignore them outright

Since `load` functions are an integral part of the framework & affect / interact with a wide range of features provided by `sveltekit` they would be hard to give up for any user of the framework. 

And ignoring them becomes quite hard as any "page" that requires `ipc` calls triggers these warnings for each individual request made.

### Additional context

Changes required would be something like this:

[ipc-protocol.js](https://github.com/tauri-apps/tauri/blob/f45ec0dcf83c139c8fdde5e61923a0e82836f756/crates/tauri/scripts/ipc-protocol.js#L37)
```ts
let trueFetch = fetch
if (options.fetchImpl !== undefined) trueFetch = options.fetchImpl

trueFetch(window.__TAURI_INTERNALS__.convertFileSrc(cmd, 'ipc'), {
``` 

[core.ts](https://github.com/tauri-apps/tauri/blob/f45ec0dcf83c139c8fdde5e61923a0e82836f756/packages/api/src/core.ts#L232)
```ts
/**
 * @since 2.0.0
 */
interface InvokeOptions {
  headers: HeadersInit
  fetchImpl?: (input: RequestInfo | URL, init?: RequestInit) => Promise<Response>
}
```
issues.title: [feat] Allow custom `fetch` impl to be passed to the `ipc` handle

issues.body:
### Describe the problem

I'm building a Tauri app for Windows and finding the current NSIS bundler a bit painful to work with when I need anything beyond the basics. NSIS scripts are hard to read and maintain, and customizing install behavior (custom pages, conditional logic, upgrade flows) quickly turns into a mess. I know I can post-process with a custom `.iss` and `iscc`, but that means losing all the native integration Tauri already has—auto-injected paths, WebView2 handling, versioning, updater markers.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Add Inno Setup as a first-class Windows bundle target (e.g. `tauri build --bundles inno`), alongside the existing NSIS and WiX options.

Inno Setup has a few things going for it that make it worth considering:

- Pascal Script is way more readable and maintainable than NSIS's stack-based syntax
- Built-in `AppId` + version upgrade handling (no manual registry gymnastics)
- Excellent silent install support out of the box (`/VERYSILENT`, `/SILENT`)
- Mature code-signing and multi-language UI
- Used by large desktop apps (VS Code, Discord, etc.) so it's well-tested in the wild

The implementation would follow the same pattern as the NSIS backend—configurable `.iss` template, variable injection from `tauri.conf.json`, invoke `iscc` during bundle, handle WebView2 bootstrapper, proper uninstall/upgrade registration.

This wouldn't replace NSIS, just give people another option.

### Alternatives considered

1. **Post-build script calling `iscc` manually** — works for a basic install/uninstall, but I lose WebView2 integration, updater bundle markers, and have to manually keep paths/versions in sync with `tauri.conf.json`. It's fragile.
2. **Stick with NSIS** — it works, but the scripting experience is rough and customizing behavior gets ugly fast.
3. **WiX/MSI** — doesn't fit my use case; I want a single exe installer, not an MSI, and WiX has its own complexity.

### Additional context

I'm aware adding another bundler means more maintenance burden on the project, so I wanted to open this as a discussion before writing any code. If the maintainers are open to it, I'd be happy to work on a PR. If not, that's totally fair—just wanted to put it out there.

From an implementation standpoint, the main pieces would be:

- New `PackageType::Inno` variant and CLI flag
- `.iss` template rendering with variable injection (app name, version, identifier → AppId, install mode, etc.)
- `iscc` discovery/invocation in the bundle step
- WebView2 bootstrapper handling (similar to how NSIS does it)
- Uninstall/upgrade registration via Inno's native `AppId` mechanism
- Config schema additions under `bundle.windows.inno.*`

I looked at [VS Code's `code.iss`](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/main/build/win32/code.iss) as a reference for how a production-grade Inno setup handles per-user/per-machine, shortcuts, file associations, and environment variables—it's a good model to follow.
issues.title: [feat] Add Inno Setup as a Windows bundling target

### Describe the problem

Google has just announced Googlebook, a new desktop platform:

https://googlebook.google/

For developers maintaining cross-platform Tauri applications, there is currently no clear guidance on how Googlebook should be targeted.

Since Tauri already supports both desktop Linux and Android, it would be useful to clarify whether Googlebook is expected to work through one of these existing targets, or whether first-class Googlebook support would require additional platform-specific integration.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Consider supporting Googlebook as an officially supported Tauri target platform, if technically feasible.

At this early stage, guidance from the Tauri team would also be helpful on the expected path for Googlebook support — for example, whether applications should target Googlebook through the existing Android or Linux support, or whether a dedicated Googlebook target and platform-specific integration may be necessary.

### Alternatives considered

One possible alternative is using Tauri's existing Android target and distributing the application as an Android application on Googlebook, assuming Googlebook provides sufficient compatibility and desktop integration.

Another possibility is using the existing Linux desktop build through Googlebook's Linux environment.

However, either approach may differ from first-class platform support in areas such as window management, filesystem access, menus, keyboard shortcuts, application lifecycle, and other desktop integrations.

### Additional context

Googlebook was announced only about 1 hour ago at the time of filing this issue, so I understand that it is extremely early and that the exact scope or feasibility of Tauri support may not yet be known.

Official Googlebook website:

https://googlebook.google/

This issue is primarily intended to start a discussion about compatibility and how the Tauri project intends to approach this new platform.

### Describe the problem

On iOS, the Tauri CLI merges `src-tauri/Info.ios.plist` into the generated `Info.plist`. Custom keys thus stay when `tauri ios init` makes the project again.

Android has no equivalent. Custom entries must go directly into `src-tauri/gen/android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml`. When `tauri android init` makes the project again, these entries are lost. You must then add them again manually.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Merge `src-tauri/AndroidManifest.xml` into the generated manifest, as the CLI does for `Info.ios.plist`. Use the Gradle manifest merger, so that `tools:node` and `tools:replace` operate as usual. Do the merge before the Gradle build starts.

```xml
<manifest xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android">
    <application>
        <activity android:name=".MainActivity">
            <intent-filter>
                <action android:name="android.intent.action.SEND" />
                <category android:name="android.intent.category.DEFAULT" />
                <data android:mimeType="text/plain" />
            </intent-filter>
        </activity>
    </application>
</manifest>
```

### Alternatives considered

- **Restore the entries from Git after each `tauri android init`.** This is manual, and it is easy to make an error.
- **Call `update_android_manifest` from the build script.** This helper only adds text between marker comments, and it runs inside the Gradle build.

### Additional context

Tauri CLI 2.11.0.
issues.title: [feat] Merge an additive AndroidManifest.xml from src-tauri, like Info.ios.plist

issues.body:
Add first-class support for Linux global application menus using the `com.canonical.AppMenu` / `com.canonical.dbusmenu` protocols, ideally at the `muda` menu layer.

The goal is for Tauri applications on supported Linux desktop environments to expose the same application menu that they use on macOS through the desktop's global menu, without requiring GTK.

<details>
<summary>Motivation</summary>

Tauri already provides a platform-independent menu API, and macOS applications can expose that menu as the native global application menu.

On Linux, however, the current menu implementation is tied to GTK/window-local menus. This means Tauri applications cannot participate in desktop environments that support the Linux global application menu ecosystem, such as KDE Plasma's global menu.

It would be useful if the existing Tauri menu model could be exposed through the standard `com.canonical.AppMenu` / `com.canonical.dbusmenu` interfaces.

This would allow an application to define its menu once:

@@@
File
Edit
View
Window
Help
@@@

and have the same menu exposed natively on each platform:

@@@
macOS   → NSApp / NSMenu
Windows → native window menu
Linux   → com.canonical.AppMenu / D-BusMenu
@@@

</details>

<details>
<summary>Proposed implementation</summary>

I believe this functionality would fit best in `muda` rather than as a Tauri-specific implementation.

Conceptually:

@@@
                    Tauri Menu API
                          │
                          ▼
                        muda
                          │
             ┌────────────┼────────────┐
             │            │            │
           macOS        Windows       Linux
             │            │            │
           NSMenu        Win32      D-BusMenu
                                      │
                                      ▼
                              AppMenu.Registrar
@@@

The Linux backend would:

1. Export the existing `muda::Menu` tree through `com.canonical.dbusmenu`.
2. Register the menu with `com.canonical.AppMenu.Registrar`.
3. Translate menu activation events back into the existing `muda` menu event mechanism.
4. Propagate menu state changes such as:
   - enabled/disabled
   - visible/hidden
   - labels
   - checked state
   - shortcuts/accelerators
   - submenu changes
5. Avoid requiring GTK for the AppMenu implementation.

This should ideally reuse the existing `muda::Menu`, `Submenu`, `MenuItem`, `PredefinedMenuItem`, etc. rather than introducing a second menu representation.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Wayland considerations</summary>

The traditional `com.canonical.AppMenu.Registrar` protocol is closely associated with X11 window IDs, so Wayland support may require additional consideration.

I would suggest initially implementing the protocol where the desktop environment provides the necessary integration, while keeping the API/backend abstract enough that Wayland-specific mechanisms can be added later.

In particular, the public API should not expose X11-specific concepts such as an XID.

Something along the lines of:

@@@
menu.set_as_app_menu(&window)?;
@@@

would be preferable to requiring applications to deal with platform-specific window identifiers.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Example API</summary>

Ideally, an application would not need to know about D-Bus or AppMenu at all.

For example:

@@@
let menu = Menu::with_items(&[
    &file_menu,
    &edit_menu,
    &view_menu,
    &window_menu,
    &help_menu,
])?;

app.set_menu(menu)?;
@@@

The platform backend would determine how the menu should be exposed.

Alternatively, if explicit opt-in is considered preferable on Linux:

@@@
menu.set_as_app_menu(&window)?;
@@@

The important part is that the same menu tree can be used on macOS and Linux rather than maintaining separate platform-specific menus.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Expected result</summary>

On a desktop environment supporting the global application menu, a Tauri application could appear approximately as:

@@@
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ MyApp   File   Edit   View   Window   Help                  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
@@@

while the application itself remains free of a GTK dependency for menu integration.

This would make Linux menu behavior much closer to the native macOS experience while preserving Tauri's cross-platform menu abstraction.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Related protocols</summary>

- `com.canonical.AppMenu.Registrar`
- `com.canonical.dbusmenu`

The implementation should follow the existing D-BusMenu/AppMenu specifications and interoperate with desktop environments that support them.

</details>

I could try to contribute an implementation if this direction is considered appropriate for the project.

issues.body:
Hello.

I have been exploring ways to package a macOS application from Linux. The dmg produced this way installs and runs on macOS. After reading the Tauri sources, I believe adding cross-compilation support to the bundler is feasible. I would like to ask whether the team is interested in this and whether a PR would be welcome.

<details>
<summary>Steps (working on Linux, artifact verified on macOS)</summary>

I cross-compile the binaries with `cross`, then assemble the `.app` and generate the dmg manually.

**1. Build the frontend on the host**

```sh
pnpm build
```

**2. Cross-compile the Rust artifacts**

```sh
cross build --release --target aarch64-apple-darwin \
    --manifest-path src-tauri/Cargo.toml \
    --features tauri/custom-protocol
```

**3. Assemble the .app directory**

The resulting layout:

```text
MyApp.app/Contents/
  Info.plist
  PkgInfo
  MacOS/my-app
  MacOS/my-sidecar
  Resources/icon.icns
```

Key `Info.plist` fields:

```xml
<key>CFBundleExecutable</key><string>my-app</string>
<key>CFBundleIdentifier</key><string>com.example.myapp</string>
<key>CFBundleShortVersionString</key><string>0.1.0</string>
<key>LSMinimumSystemVersion</key><string>11.0</string>
<key>CFBundleURLTypes</key>
<array><dict>
  <key>CFBundleURLSchemes</key>
  <array><string>myapp</string></array>
</dict></array>
```

**4. Sign and generate the dmg**

`rcodesign` provides the ad-hoc signature, `genisoimage -apple` produces the image, and the `dmg` tool from libdmg-hfsplus converts it to UDIF:

```sh
rcodesign sign MyApp.app

genisoimage -no-cache-inodes -D -l -probe -V MyApp -no-pad -r -dir-mode 0755 \
  -apple -o myapp.iso stage/
dmg myapp.iso myapp_0.1.0_aarch64.dmg
```

The artifact installs and starts on macOS, and its Tauri IPC calls to the backend behave as expected.

</details>

After reviewing the code, I believe the following changes are needed to bring this into Tauri.

<details>
<summary>Steps to integrate into Tauri</summary>

**1. Remove the conditional compilation from the bundle module**

`mod macos` in `crates/tauri-bundler/src/bundle.rs` and the `MacOsBundle` and `Dmg` entries in `ALL_PACKAGE_TYPES` in `settings.rs` carry `#[cfg(target_os = "macos")]`. Removing these conditions makes `app` and `dmg` available to `--bundles` on a Linux host. `BundleFormat::value_variants` in the CLI projects `PackageType::all()` directly, so the CLI needs no changes.

**2. Add a Linux implementation to the bundle dispatch**

The bundle dispatch selects a backend based on `settings.target_platform()`, keeping the existing implementation for a macOS host and using the new one for a Linux host. `Info.plist` would be generated through the `plist` crate, icons continue to use `create_icns_file`, and the `externalBin` copy logic is reusable across platforms.

**3. Use rcodesign for signing on Linux**

`macos/sign.rs` depends on `tauri-macos-sign`, which is only pulled in for macOS targets. A Linux host would invoke `rcodesign` to sign instead.

**4. Use genisoimage -apple plus udif for the dmg**

The Linux backend builds the image with `genisoimage -apple` and wraps it as UDIF through the `udif` crate, replacing `hdiutil` and `osascript`. The Finder icon layout, window size, and background image settings would not be available.

**5. Distribute the host tools**

The extra binaries on a Linux host follow the NSIS mechanism: a tarball with a SHA checksum is downloaded to `~/.cache/tauri/`, and `bundle.useLocalToolsDir` points at a local directory. Inlining signing and UDIF wrapping as Rust dependencies leaves only one static `genisoimage` binary to distribute.

**6. Land it in stages**

Start with `--bundles app`, which is almost entirely pure Rust logic and the cheapest to verify. The dmg follows, with signing and notarization last.

</details>

**Current limitations**

- `Assets.car` requires `actool` from Xcode, so a Linux host keeps the existing skip behavior.
- The Finder layout of the dmg is not available on a Linux host.
- Notarization requires Apple service credentials, so the first stage covers signing only.
- `validate_target` checks whether the rustup target is installed, which `rustup target add aarch64-apple-darwin` on the host satisfies.
issues.title: [feat] Support building macOS .app and .dmg bundles from a Linux host

issues.body: ### Describe the problem Foldable phones change the layout that an app must follow. A Tauri app shows its bars in HTML. Thus, the app does not get this layout, on iOS or on Android. - **iOS (iPhone Duo):** In some poses, iOS moves the app bars to one side of the display. When the device is partially folded, iOS also identifies the hinge as a reserved region. Native apps get this layout from `UINavigationController` and `NavigationStack`. `WKWebView` gives only the safe-area insets. The insets do not tell the page if the bars are vertical, which edge they are on, or where the fold is. - **Android foldables:** Android reports the hinge and the posture through Jetpack WindowManager (`FoldingFeature`). Native apps use these values to keep content off the hinge and to split the layout in the tabletop and book postures. The safe-area insets in the WebView do not include the hinge. Apple guidance: [Preparing your app for iPhone Duo](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/technologyoverviews/preparing-your-app-for-iphone-duo) Android guidance: [Make your app fold aware](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/layouts/adaptive/foldables/make-your-app-fold-aware) ### Describe the solution you'd like The fix is in the webviews, not in Tauri: - **Fold and posture:** The Viewport Segments API and the Device Posture API give the page the fold position and the posture. - **iOS:** Safari 27.1 has a developer preview of both APIs ([WebKit Features for Safari 27.1](https://webkit.org/blog/18486/webkit-features-for-safari-27-1/)). WebKit must make these APIs available in `WKWebView`. - **Android:** Chrome ships the Device Posture API (Chrome 132) and the Viewport Segments API (Chrome 138). When the Device Posture API shipped, it was disabled in Android WebView ([crbug 335314107](https://issues.chromium.org/issues/335314107)). Android WebView must make both APIs available. - **Vertical bar edge (iOS only):** No web standard gives this value. WebKit must add one, for example an `env()` variable. Android does not move the app bars, so it needs no equivalent. ### Alternatives considered - **A native Tauri plugin.** On iOS, the plugin reads the `verticalBarEdge` trait and the reserved regions in Swift. On Android, it reads `FoldingFeature` from Jetpack WindowManager in Kotlin. The plugin sends these values to the page. It can use the names from the web specifications, so that apps can remove the plugin when the webviews add this support. - **Native bars.** Each app must then keep a second bar implementation for each platform, for example in a `UINavigationController` on iOS. - **Device detection with fixed inset values.** This does not operate correctly in all poses or on future devices. ### Additional context Related: #6030 (native window dimensions as `env()` values) and #11475 (safe-area control on iOS and Android).
issues.title: [feat] detect foldable displays and support layout adaptation

Versions: tauri 2.12.4 (also 2.12.5) · tauri-runtime-wry 2.12.2 (also 2.12.3 and `dev`)

`tauri::webview::NewWindowResponse::Create { window: WebviewWindow }` is mapped to
`tauri_runtime::webview::NewWindowResponse::Create { window_id }` (`crates/tauri/src/webview/mod.rs`, ~L775), and
tauri-runtime-wry then hands wry the first webview of that window (`.webviews.first()`, ~L4860).

wry itself accepts any platform webview built with the opener's configuration
(`wry::NewWindowResponse::Create { webview }` — macOS: same `WKWebViewConfiguration`; Windows: same environment),
and tauri already lets a child webview be built that way (`WebviewBuilder::with_webview_configuration`, ~L1414).

So an app whose tabs are child webviews of one main window (`Window::add_child`) cannot answer a script's
`window.open(url, name)` with a new tab: returning the main window would hand WebKit the app's own UI webview.
Opening its own tab instead leaves the page unrelated to it — `window.opener` is `null`, and the usual
"choose in the popup, send the choice back to the opener" flow does nothing.

Suggestion (maintainers' call): a response variant that takes a `Webview` (looked up by webview id rather than
window id), e.g. `NewWindowResponse::CreateWebview { webview }`, documented with the same configuration /
environment requirement. The window case stays as it is.

Related: #14318 (how to keep `window.opener` with multiple windows).
issues.title: on_new_window: allow answering with a Webview, so a child-webview app can hand a script-opened tab back to the opener
